para_before: In the CHALLENGE trial, structured exercise for 3 years after adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer prolonged disease-free survival, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.72 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.55–0.94) [9]. In breast cancer, randomized trials of exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy improved physical fitness and, in some, fatigue [10–13], and an exploratory follow-up of one trial found an HR for disease-free survival of 0.68 (95% CI 0.37–1.24) [14]. During neoadjuvant chemotherapy, diet and exercise were associated with a higher pCR in one trial [15], supervised exercise did not change tumor size in two others [16,17], and a meta-analysis across cancer types found no difference in pCR [18]. A trial powered for pCR, with disease-free survival as a secondary outcome, is ongoing [19]. None of these trials reported recurrence, so the effect of exercise during neoadjuvant chemotherapy on recurrence is unknown.

para_before: Economic evaluations of exercise in cancer have valued effects on fatigue, fitness or quality of life during or after adjuvant treatment [20–22], and in breast cancer they reached different conclusions [23–25]. No economic evaluation of exercise during neoadjuvant therapy for breast cancer was identified; the nearest, Phys-Can, compared two exercise intensities during treatment of breast, colorectal or prostate cancer [26]. When an effect is unknown, a cost-effectiveness ratio cannot be estimated, but the highest program cost that remains cost-effective can be calculated for each possible effect [27]. Cost-effectiveness analyses of the KEYNOTE-522 regimen come from the United States, Hong Kong, Switzerland and Egypt [28–31], whereas Japanese analyses have concerned pembrolizumab for advanced cancers, including metastatic TNBC [32–38], and the perioperative TNBC indication has not been assessed in Japan's cost-effectiveness evaluation [39].
para_after: Economic evaluations of exercise in cancer have valued effects on fatigue, fitness or quality of life during or after adjuvant treatment [20–22], and in breast cancer they reached different conclusions [23–25]. Searches of PubMed and Europe PMC covering 2000 to 2026 identified no economic evaluation of exercise during neoadjuvant therapy for breast cancer (Supplementary Methods S1); the nearest, Phys-Can, compared two exercise intensities during treatment of breast, colorectal or prostate cancer [26]. When an effect is unknown, a cost-effectiveness ratio cannot be estimated, but the highest program cost that remains cost-effective can be calculated for each possible effect [27]. Cost-effectiveness analyses of the KEYNOTE-522 regimen come from the United States, Hong Kong, Switzerland and Egypt [28–31], whereas Japanese analyses have concerned pembrolizumab for advanced cancers, including metastatic TNBC [32–38], and the perioperative TNBC indication has not been assessed in Japan's cost-effectiveness evaluation [39].

para_before: The exposure was the recurrence HR with exercise: the HR for locoregional and distant recurrence after surgery in an arm with exercise, relative to the same treatment without exercise (Table 1). It ranged from 0.70 to 1.00 and did not act on deaths without recurrence or on events before surgery. The CHALLENGE estimate of 0.72 served as a reference point [9]. In the base case, the HR held for 5 years after randomization and the effect then halved every year. Alternative durations held it until 1 year after surgery or for life; in a further alternative, exercise continued for 30 months after surgery at additional cost, and the effect held until it stopped. In an alternative pathway, exercise raised pCR by 0 to 10 percentage points without changing the recurrence HR. Musculoskeletal adverse events occurred at the rates observed in CHALLENGE [9].

old_paragraphs: The model used 1-month cycles from the start of neoadjuvant therapy to age 100 years, with the cohort split by pCR at surgery in month 7 (Fig. 1). The survival model was built without overall survival, which served only to validate the model against acceptance criteria fixed before each comparison [5,44] (Supplementary Methods; Fig. S1; Table S3).

The model was run at recurrence HRs from 0.70 to 1.00 in steps of 0.025 and at pCR increases from 0 to 10 percentage points. Break-even HRs and the exercise effect matching pembrolizumab were found numerically. Each of 1,000 probabilistic samples paired one bootstrap replicate of the survival model with one draw of cost and utility inputs, using gamma distributions for costs and durations, beta distributions for proportions and utilities and lognormal distributions for HRs; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles gave the 95% uncertainty interval (UI). One-way sensitivity analyses set each input to its bounds; where a source gave no range, it was ±25% or mirrored, and drug prices varied downward only, to 75% of the list price.

Scenario analyses changed one assumption at a time (Table 1): utility values from the United States, United Kingdom and Australian analyses [28,29,65]; higher excess mortality after early recurrence with pembrolizumab, from an Italian cohort [66]; longer survival after progression during neoadjuvant therapy [67]; halved costs of metastatic treatment; eribulin-based later-line treatment [68]; and post-operative capecitabine or olaparib for patients without pCR [69–71]. The one-year net benefit used the fee-schedule-based program at recurrence HRs of 0.95, 0.90 and 0.85, applying the main comparison to patients who received neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in the 2024 national registry and the secondary comparison to the others [7]; these values are conditional on the HR. Analyses were performed in R version 4.5.1.
new_paragraphs: The model used 1-month cycles from the start of neoadjuvant therapy to age 100 years, with the cohort split by pCR at surgery in month 7 (Fig. 1).

(1) To check that the model reproduced the trial, overall survival, which was not used to build the survival model, was compared with KEYNOTE-522 against acceptance criteria fixed before each comparison [5,44] (Supplementary Methods S1; Fig. S1; Table S3).

(2) To estimate the maximum affordable cost, the model was run at recurrence HRs from 0.70 to 1.00 in steps of 0.025 and at increases in pCR from 0 to 10 percentage points in steps of 1. Break-even HRs and the exercise effect matching the QALY gain of pembrolizumab were found numerically, over HRs from 0.30 to 1.00 and increases in pCR of up to 37 percentage points.

(3) To reflect uncertainty, each of 1,000 probabilistic samples paired one bootstrap replicate of the survival model with one draw of the other inputs. Costs, durations and events per patient followed gamma distributions, proportions and utilities beta distributions, and HRs lognormal distributions; drug prices and rates based on zero events were fixed. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the samples gave the 95% uncertainty interval (UI). The probability that a program was cost-effective was the share of samples in which the maximum affordable cost exceeded the program cost. For pembrolizumab, it was the share of samples with a positive net monetary benefit at each threshold.

(4) To find the inputs that move the results most, one-way sensitivity analyses set each input to its lower and upper bounds, for the maximum affordable cost in the main comparison at an HR of 0.85 and for the ICER of pembrolizumab. Where a source gave no range, the range was ±25% of the base value or the missing bound mirrored the given one; drug prices varied downward only, to 75% of the list price.

(5) To test other assumptions, scenario analyses changed one assumption at a time (Table 1): utility values from the United States, United Kingdom and Australian analyses [28,29,65]; higher excess mortality after early recurrence with pembrolizumab, from an Italian cohort [66]; longer survival after progression during neoadjuvant therapy [67]; halved costs of metastatic treatment; eribulin-based later-line treatment [68]; and post-operative capecitabine or olaparib for patients without pCR [69–71].

(6) To express the result for Japan, the one-year net benefit used the fee-schedule-based program at recurrence HRs of 0.95, 0.90 and 0.85, applying the main comparison to patients who received neoadjuvant pembrolizumab in the 2024 national registry and the secondary comparison to the others [7]; these values are conditional on the HR.
Analyses were performed in R version 4.5.1.

old: For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation.
new: For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation of its perioperative indication.
para_before: Exercise during adjuvant chemotherapy improves fitness [10–12], and supervised exercise has been delivered during neoadjuvant chemotherapy [16,17], so clinicians can offer it while its effect on recurrence is tested. Trials should record recurrence and follow patients long enough to see whether the effect lasts after the program ends; a higher pCR alone cannot settle the question, because how a change in pCR with exercise translates into fewer recurrences is unknown. Funders can weigh the cost of such trials against the one-year net benefit if an effect is confirmed (Table S8). For payers, the price of a supervised program is far below what a confirmed effect would justify. In Japan, the fee schedule pays for rehabilitation of patients with cancer only during hospital admission, so structured exercise during outpatient neoadjuvant chemotherapy currently has no route to reimbursement [48]. Support that keeps patients exercising after surgery, such as remote programs, would add value if it extends the effect (Table S7). For pembrolizumab, this analysis gives Japan a reference value before any formal evaluation.

para_before: Results Added to chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab, exercise had a maximum affordable cost of JPY 2,726 thousand per patient at an HR of 0.85 (95% uncertainty interval 2,223–3,040). Added to chemotherapy alone, it was JPY 3,443 thousand. A program priced from the medical fee schedule (JPY 192,400) became cost-effective at an HR of 0.989. Medical costs avoided alone paid for it at HRs of 0.958 to 0.914, depending on metastatic treatment costs. The duration of the effect changed the maximum affordable cost more than any cost input. Pembrolizumab cost JPY 2,053 thousand per QALY gained, and exercise would need an HR of 0.425 to match its QALY gain.

para_before: The maximum affordable cost rose as the recurrence HR with exercise fell (Fig. 2). At an HR of 0.85, exercise added to chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab had a maximum affordable cost of JPY 2,726 thousand per patient (95% UI 2,223–3,040; Table 2), and at 0.70 it was JPY 5,596 thousand (95% UI 4,545–6,256; Table S4). The maximum affordable cost equaled the cost of the fee-schedule-based program at an HR of 0.989, a 1.1% reduction in the recurrence hazard, and medical costs avoided equaled it at an HR of 0.958, a 4.2% reduction (Table 2). Through pCR, an increase of 1 percentage point gave JPY 389 thousand (95% UI 238–570) and 10 points gave JPY 3,898 thousand (95% UI 2,388–5,713; Table S5).

para_before: Pembrolizumab added JPY 4,426 thousand per patient in costs (95% UI −330 to 8,901) and 2.156 QALYs (95% UI 0.245–4.228), for an ICER of JPY 2,053 thousand per QALY (Table 3). Its drug cost was JPY 6,531 thousand, offset partly by JPY −1,911 thousand in second-line and later treatment of distant recurrence.
